title: Impedance Matching
description: L-sections, single-stub tuners, quarter-wave and multi-section transformers, and the bandwidth they buy.

study.title: Why and how to match
study.body: A matching network sits between a $Z_0$ line and a load $Z_L$ so that the line sees $Z_0$: no reflection, maximum power to the load, and for receivers a better noise figure. It must be **lossless** (only L, C, lines and stubs), so it can only move the load around the Smith chart, not absorb power. Any lossless network matches at one frequency; the art is to keep the match over the needed **bandwidth**.

study.title: L-sections: which topology?
study.body:
Two reactances, one series and one shunt. Which one goes next to the load depends on where $z_L$ sits:
- inside the $r$ = 1 circle ($R_L > Z_0$): **shunt** element across the load, series element toward the line
- inside the $g$ = 1 circle (dashed, $G_L > Y_0$): **series** element at the load, shunt element across the line
- outside both: either works.
Each topology has two solutions. On the chart a series L or shunt C moves the point clockwise (along constant $r$ or constant $g$), a series C or shunt L counter-clockwise.

study.title: L-section with the series element at the load ($R_L < Z_0$)
study.body: The series reactance $X$ first moves the load onto the circle where $Y = 1/Z_0 + jB'$; the shunt susceptance $B$ then cancels $B'$. Choose the upper or lower signs together. Positive $X$ is an inductor ($L = X/\omega$), negative a capacitor ($C = -1/\omega X$); positive $B$ is a capacitor ($C = B/\omega$), negative an inductor ($L = -1/\omega B$).

study.title: L-section with the shunt element at the load ($R_L > Z_0$)
study.body: The shunt susceptance $B$ across the load moves it onto the circle $R = Z_0$; the series reactance $X$ then cancels what is left. Both signs of the square root give a solution. Since $R_L > Z_0$ the root is always real, and the + sign gives $B > 0$ (a shunt capacitor).
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& q = \sqrt{\tfrac{R_L}{Z_0}\left(R_L^2 + X_L^2 - Z_0R_L\right)}\\ & B = \frac{X_L \pm q}{R_L^2 + X_L^2}\\ & X = \frac{1}{B} + \frac{X_LZ_0}{R_L} - \frac{Z_0}{BR_L}\end{aligned}

study.title: Worked example: L-section
study.body:
Match $Z_L$ = 100 + j50 Ω to 50 Ω at 1 GHz. $R_L > Z_0$, so the shunt element goes across the load.
- $R_L^2 + X_L^2$ = 12 500, $\sqrt{R_L/Z_0}$ = 1.414, $\sqrt{R_L^2 + X_L^2 - Z_0R_L}$ = 86.6
- + sign: $B$ = (50 + 122.5)/12 500 = 13.8 mS, $X$ = 72.5 + 25 − 36.2 = +61.2 Ω
- Shunt C = B/ω = 2.20 pF, series L = X/ω = 9.75 nH
- − sign: $B$ = −5.80 mS (shunt L = 27.4 nH), $X$ = −61.2 Ω (series C = 2.60 pF)
The low-pass solution (series L, shunt C) also attenuates harmonics.

study.title: Single-stub shunt tuning
study.body: Move along the line until the admittance has $g$ = 1: $y = 1 + jb$. A shunt stub with susceptance $-jb$ placed there cancels $b$. On the chart, rotate the load clockwise on its SWR circle to the dashed $g$ = 1 circle; there are two crossings per λ/2. With Γ = |Γ|∠θ at the load, the crossings are at angles φ with cos φ = −|Γ|, reached after $d = (\theta - \varphi)/720°$ wavelengths (add 0.5 λ if negative), and there $b = -2|\Gamma|\sin\varphi/(1-|\Gamma|^2)$. Example: $Z_L$ = 30 − j60 Ω has Γ = 0.2 − j0.6 = 0.632∠−71.6°, so φ = ±129.2°: $d$ = 0.080 λ ($y$ = 1 + j1.63, shorted stub 0.0875 λ) or $d$ = 0.221 λ ($y$ = 1 − j1.63, open stub 0.163 λ).

study.title: Quarter-wave transformer and its bandwidth
study.body: A λ/4 section of $Z_1 = \sqrt{Z_0R_L}$ matches a **real** load (put a complex load first at a voltage maximum or minimum with a piece of line). Away from $f_0$ the section is no longer λ/4 and the match degrades. For a maximum tolerable $\Gamma_m$ the fractional bandwidth follows from the band edge $\theta_m$ (TEM line, θ = π/2 at $f_0$). The larger the ratio $R_L/Z_0$, the narrower the band: compare 100 Ω (green) and 200 Ω (orange) loads.

study.title: Explore: more sections, more bandwidth
study.body: Several λ/4 sections in a row each reflect a little; small-reflection theory adds these partial reflections. Choosing them in binomial proportions gives the **maximally flat** (binomial) transformer: $|\Gamma| \approx |\Gamma_L|\,|\cos\theta|^N$. For two sections $Z_1 = Z_0(R_L/Z_0)^{1/4}$ and $Z_2 = Z_0(R_L/Z_0)^{3/4}$. Drag $N$ for a 100 Ω load on 50 Ω and watch the bandwidth for $\Gamma_m$ = 0.1 grow (the price is a longer transformer).

steps.title: Two reactances
steps.body: An L-section uses one series and one shunt reactance. Which goes next to the load depends on the load: inside the $r$ = 1 circle ($R_L > Z_0$) the shunt element must sit across the load; inside the $g$ = 1 circle (where $G_L > 1/Z_0$) the series element must sit at the load. Elsewhere both topologies work.

derived.g: if(k, ra, rb)/(if(k, ra, rb)^2+if(k, xa, 0.3*sb)^2)

steps.prompt: The red dot is a load $z_L$ (the dashed circle is $g$ = 1). Which L-section topology can match it to $Z_0$?
options: Shunt element across the load, series element toward the line
Series element at the load, shunt element across the line
Neither: this load needs a stub
steps.explanation: The load is $z_L$ = {{r}} + j({{x}}), so $r$ = {{r}} and $g = r/(r^2 + x^2)$ = {{g}}. Inside the $r$ = 1 circle ($r$ > 1) a series element alone can never reach $r$ = 1, so a shunt element must act first. Inside the $g$ = 1 circle ($g$ > 1) a shunt element can never reach $g$ = 1, so a series element must act first. Every load with $r$ > 0 can be matched by an L-section.

steps.title: Series element at the load ($R_L < Z_0$)
steps.body: The series $X$ moves the load to $R_L + j\sqrt{R_L(Z_0-R_L)}$ (or its conjugate), whose admittance has real part exactly $1/Z_0$. The shunt $B$ then cancels the leftover susceptance. Take the upper signs together or the lower signs together.

steps.prompt: Match $Z_L$ = {{RL}} + j({{XL}}) Ω to 50 Ω with an L-section: series reactance $X$ at the load, shunt susceptance $B$ across the line. Use the solution with a shunt **capacitor** ($B$ > 0).

ask.prompt: Find the series reactance $X$ (with sign).
ask.explanation: $\sqrt{R_L(Z_0 - R_L)}$ = √({{RL}} × {{50-RL}}) = {{rt}} Ω. With the upper sign: $X$ = {{rt}} − ({{XL}}) = **{{X|Ω}}** (positive: series inductor; negative: series capacitor).

ask.prompt: Find the shunt susceptance $B$.
ask.explanation: $B = \frac{1}{Z_0}\sqrt{\frac{Z_0 - R_L}{R_L}}$ = (1/50) × √({{50-RL}}/{{RL}}) = **{{B|S}}**: a shunt capacitor. Check: after the series element the load is {{RL}} + j{{rt}} Ω, whose admittance is {{RL/(RL^2+rt^2)|S}} − j{{rt/(RL^2+rt^2)|S}}; the shunt B cancels the imaginary part and 1/50 = 20 mS remains.

steps.title: Shunt element at the load ($R_L > Z_0$)
steps.body: Now the shunt $B$ across the load brings the real part of the impedance down to exactly $Z_0$, and the series $X$ cancels the remaining reactance. The + sign always gives $B > 0$, a shunt capacitor.
steps.formula: \begin{aligned}& q = \sqrt{\tfrac{R_L}{Z_0}\left(R_L^2 + X_L^2 - Z_0R_L\right)}\\ & B = \frac{X_L \pm q}{R_L^2 + X_L^2}\\ & X = \frac{1}{B} + \frac{X_LZ_0}{R_L} - \frac{Z_0}{BR_L}\end{aligned}

steps.prompt: Match $Z_L$ = {{RL}} + j({{XL}}) Ω to 50 Ω with a shunt susceptance $B$ across the load and a series reactance $X$ toward the line. Use the + sign (shunt capacitor).

ask.prompt: Find $B$.
Find $X$ (with sign).
ask.explanation: $B$ = ({{XL}} + {{sq}}) / {{m||5}} = {{B|S}}. Then $X = 1/B + X_LZ_0/R_L - Z_0/(BR_L)$ = {{1/B}} + {{XL*50/RL}} − {{50/(B*RL)}} = **{{X|Ω}}** (positive: series inductor, negative: series capacitor).

steps.prompt: Match each result of an L-section design to the component you build.
steps.explanation: An inductor has $Z = j\omega L$ (positive reactance) and admittance $-j/(\omega L)$ (negative susceptance); a capacitor has $Z = -j/(\omega C)$ and $Y = j\omega C$. So the sign tells you the element, and ω turns the number into a value.

steps.prompt: An L-section design at {{f|Hz}} needs a series reactance of +{{X}} Ω and a shunt susceptance of +{{B|S}}.

ask.prompt: Which series inductance do you need?
Which shunt capacitance do you need?

steps.prompt: Every load with a positive resistance can be matched to $Z_0$ by at least one of the two L-section topologies.
steps.explanation: True. If $R_L > Z_0$ the shunt-first topology always has a real solution; if $R_L < Z_0$ the series-first topology always does. Only a lossless load (on the rim of the chart) cannot be matched, because there is no power to deliver.

steps.title: Line plus one stub
steps.body: At microwave frequencies lumped L and C are hard to build, so use lines: a length $d$ of line rotates the load until its admittance is $y = 1 + jb$, and a shunt stub of susceptance $-jb$ placed there cancels $b$. On the chart: rotate clockwise on the SWR circle until you hit the dashed $g$ = 1 circle (the $r$ = 1 circle mirrored through the centre).

steps.prompt: The load $z_L$ = {{r}} + j({{x}}) is blue. Drag the distance $d$ until the red point lies on the dashed $g$ = 1 circle, so that $y = 1 + jb$.
steps.explanation: $\Gamma_L$ = {{G}}∠{{deg(th)}}°. The SWR circle meets the $g$ = 1 circle where cos φ = −|Γ|, i.e. at φ = ±{{deg(acos(-G))}}°. Rotating clockwise from {{deg(th)}}° to these angles takes $d$ = **{{d1}} λ** (there $y$ = 1 − j{{2*G/sqrt(1-G^2)}}) or **{{d2}} λ** ($y$ = 1 + j{{2*G/sqrt(1-G^2)}}).

steps.title: The numbers behind the chart
steps.body: With $\Gamma_L = |\Gamma|∠\theta$, the point reaches $g$ = 1 at angles φ with cos φ = −|Γ|, after $d = (\theta - \varphi)/720°$ wavelengths (add 0.5 λ if negative). There the susceptance is $b = -2|\Gamma|\sin\varphi/(1 - |\Gamma|^2)$: the upper crossing (φ > 0) gives $b < 0$, the lower one $b > 0$. The stub must supply $-b$.

steps.prompt: A single shunt stub must match $Z_L$ = {{R}} + j({{X}}) Ω to a 50 Ω line. Use the stub position **closest** to the load.

ask.prompt: How far from the load (in wavelengths) is the stub?
ask.explanation: $\Gamma_L$ = {{gr}} + j({{gi}}) = {{G}}∠{{deg(th)}}°. The $g$ = 1 crossings are at φ = ±arccos(−{{G}}) = ±{{deg(p1)}}°. Clockwise from {{deg(th)}}°: $d_1$ = {{d1}} λ (to +{{deg(p1)}}°) and $d_2$ = {{d2}} λ (to −{{deg(p1)}}°). The closer one is **{{ds}} λ**.

ask.prompt: What normalized susceptance $b$ does the line show there (with sign)?
ask.explanation: The nearest crossing is at $d$ = {{ds}} λ. There $|b| = 2|\Gamma|/\sqrt{1-|\Gamma|^2}$ = 2 × {{G}} / {{sqrt(1-G^2)}} = {{bm}}; the upper crossing has $b$ < 0, the lower one $b$ > 0, so $b$ = **{{bs}}**. The stub must add {{-bs}}.

steps.prompt: At the stub position the line shows $y$ = 1 + j({{b}}). The stub must add $-jb$.

ask.prompt: How long (in wavelengths) is the shortest **shorted** stub that does this?
ask.explanation: A shorted stub has $y_s = -j\cot\beta\ell$. We need $-\cot\beta\ell$ = {{-b}}, so $\cot\beta\ell$ = {{b}} and βℓ = arctan(1/{{b}}) = {{deg(atan(1/b))}}° (add 180° if negative). ℓ/λ = **{{mod(atan(1/b)/(2*pi), 0.5)}}**.

ask.prompt: How long (in wavelengths) is the shortest **open** stub that does this?
ask.explanation: An open stub has $y_s = j\tan\beta\ell$. We need $\tan\beta\ell$ = {{-b}}, so βℓ = arctan({{-b}}) = {{deg(atan(-b))}}° (add 180° if negative). ℓ/λ = **{{mod(atan(-b)/(2*pi), 0.5)}}**.

steps.prompt: At the stub position $y$ = 1 + j({{b}}). Which stub **shorter than λ/4** cancels the susceptance?
options: An open stub (it is capacitive below λ/4)
A shorted stub (it is inductive below λ/4)
steps.explanation: The stub must add {{-b}} to $b$. Positive susceptance is capacitive: an open stub below λ/4 ($y = j\tan\beta\ell$). Negative susceptance is inductive: a shorted stub below λ/4 ($y = -j\cot\beta\ell$). Here the stub must supply {{-b}}: a positive value calls for an open stub, a negative one for a shorted stub.

steps.prompt: In microstrip, open-circuited stubs are usually preferred because they need no via to ground.
steps.explanation: True. A shorted microstrip stub needs a via hole, which adds inductance and cost. In coax or waveguide it is the other way round: an open end radiates and is ill-defined, so shorted stubs are preferred.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a single-stub shunt design in order.
items: Rotate clockwise to the $g$ = 1 circle: this gives $d$ and $y = 1 + jb$
Choose a shorted or open stub with susceptance $-jb$
Convert $d$ and the stub length to millimetres with $\lambda$ on the line
steps.explanation: Everything starts from the normalized load. Its SWR circle holds every impedance along the line; the crossings with $g$ = 1 are the only places where a shunt element can finish the match. The stub then cancels $jb$, and finally the electrical lengths become physical lengths using the wavelength on that line.

steps.prompt: A microstrip λ/4 transformer must match a {{RL|Ω}} resistive load to a 50 Ω line at {{f|Hz}}. The effective permittivity of the strip is {{ee}}.

ask.prompt: What characteristic impedance does the section need?
How long is the section?
ask.explanation: On the strip $\lambda = c/(f\sqrt{\varepsilon_{eff}})$ = 3 × $10^8$ / ({{f|Hz}} × √{{ee}}) = {{3e8/(f*sqrt(ee))|m}}, so λ/4 = **{{3e8/(4*f*sqrt(ee))|m}}**.

steps.prompt: A single λ/4 transformer matches {{RL|Ω}} to 50 Ω. Over what fractional bandwidth (in %) is $|\Gamma|$ ≤ {{Gm}}?
The graph shows |Γ| of a λ/4 transformer from 50 Ω to {{RL|Ω}}. Drag the marker to the **upper** band edge, where |Γ| rises to {{Gm}} (dashed line).
steps.explanation: The band edges are at $\theta_m$ and $\pi - \theta_m$ with $\cos\theta_m = \frac{2\Gamma_m}{\sqrt{1-\Gamma_m^2}}\frac{\sqrt{Z_0R_L}}{|R_L - Z_0|}$, giving $\theta_m$ = {{deg(tm)}}°. Since θ = 90° · $f/f_0$, the upper edge is at $f/f_0 = 2 - \theta_m/90°$ = **{{fu}}**, the bandwidth {{100*(2-4*tm/pi)}} %.

steps.prompt: Design a two-section binomial transformer from 50 Ω to {{RL|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find $Z_1$ (the section next to the 50 Ω line).
Find $Z_2$ (the section next to the load).

steps.prompt: A {{N}}-section binomial transformer matches {{RL|Ω}} to 50 Ω. Estimate the fractional bandwidth (in %) for $|\Gamma|$ ≤ {{Gm}}.
A PA output of {{RL}} Ω must be matched to 50 Ω with lumped L-networks.

ask.prompt: What is the node Q of a single L-section?
ask.explanation: $Q_n = \sqrt{R_{high}/R_{low} - 1}$ = √(50/{{RL}} − 1) = **{{sqrt(50/RL-1)}}**. Half-power bandwidth is roughly $2f_0/Q_n$ for $Q_n$ above about 3.

ask.prompt: With two L-sections through an intermediate $R_v = \sqrt{R_{low}R_{high}}$, what is the Q of each section?
ask.explanation: $R_v$ = √({{RL}} × 50) = {{sqrt(50*RL)|Ω}}, so each section transforms by √(50/{{RL}}) = {{sqrt(50/RL)}}: $Q$ = √({{sqrt(50/RL)}} − 1) = **{{sqrt(sqrt(50/RL)-1)}}** instead of {{sqrt(50/RL-1)}}. Lower Q, wider bandwidth.

steps.prompt: The larger the ratio $R_{high}/R_{low}$ an L-section has to transform, the higher its Q and the narrower its bandwidth.
steps.explanation: True. $Q_n = \sqrt{R_{high}/R_{low} - 1}$ grows with the ratio, and a higher Q means a narrower band. Large ratios are therefore split into several sections (or a λ/4 multi-section transformer).

steps.prompt: Match each matching technique to its key property.
pairs: Line length plus one shunt stub
steps.explanation: An L-section uses one series and one shunt L or C. A stub tuner replaces them by a line length and a stub. The λ/4 transformer needs a real load (or a line in front to make it real). Several binomial sections spread the transformation, giving a flat response over a wider band.

steps.prompt: A transistor input is $Z_L$ = {{R}} + j({{X}}) Ω at {{f|Hz}}. Match it to 50 Ω with a series inductor at the transistor and a shunt capacitor across the 50 Ω side.

ask.prompt: Find the series inductance.
ask.explanation: $R_L < Z_0$, so the series element sits at the load: $X = \sqrt{R_L(Z_0-R_L)} - X_L$ = {{rt}} − ({{X}}) = {{Xs|Ω}}. $L = X/\omega$ = {{Xs}} / (2π × {{f|Hz}}) = **{{Xs/w|H}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the shunt capacitance.

steps.prompt: A microstrip single-stub tuner ($\varepsilon_{eff}$ = {{ee}}) must match $Z_L$ = {{R}} + j({{X}}) Ω to 50 Ω at {{f|Hz}}, with the stub as close to the load as possible and a **shorted** stub.

ask.prompt: How far from the load is the stub, in mm?
ask.explanation: $\Gamma_L$ = {{G}}∠{{deg(th)}}°; the $g$ = 1 crossings lie at $d$ = {{d1}} λ and {{d2}} λ; the nearer is {{ds}} λ. λ on the strip = 3 × $10^8$/({{f|Hz}} × √{{ee}}) = {{lam|m}}, so $d$ = **{{ds*lam|m}}**.

ask.prompt: How long is the shorted stub, in mm?
ask.explanation: At $d$ = {{ds}} λ the line shows $y$ = 1 + j({{bs}}). The shorted stub must give $-\cot\beta\ell$ = {{-bs}}: βℓ = arctan(1/{{bs}}) (+180° if negative), ℓ = {{ls}} λ = **{{ls*lam|m}}** with λ = {{lam|m}}.

steps.prompt: An inductive load $z_L$ = {{r}} + j{{x}} on a 50 Ω line is matched with a λ/4 transformer placed at the first voltage **maximum**.

ask.prompt: How far from the load (in wavelengths) is that maximum?
ask.explanation: $\Gamma_L$ = {{G}}∠{{deg(th)}}°. The maximum is where the SWR circle crosses the positive real axis: after a clockwise turn of {{deg(th)}}°, i.e. ℓ = {{deg(th)}}/720 = **{{th/(4*pi)}} λ**.

ask.prompt: What characteristic impedance must the λ/4 section have?
ask.explanation: At the maximum the line shows $R = Z_0\cdot VSWR$ with VSWR = (1 + {{G}})/(1 − {{G}}) = {{S}}: $R$ = {{50*S|Ω}}. $Z_1 = \sqrt{50R} = Z_0\sqrt{VSWR}$ = **{{50*sqrt(S)|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: Match $z_L$ = {{r}} + j({{x}}) (blue) with a series reactance $x_s$ at the load followed by a shunt **capacitor** $b_s$ > 0. Orange shows the series step, purple the shunt step. Drag both until the end point (red) sits in the centre.
steps.explanation: Normalized ($Z_0$ = 1): $x_s = \sqrt{r(1-r)} - x$ = {{sqrt(r*(1-r))}} − ({{x}}) = **{{xt}}** moves the load along its $r$ circle onto the $g$ = 1 circle, where $y$ = 1 − j{{bt}}. The shunt capacitor $b_s = \sqrt{(1-r)/r}$ = **{{bt}}** then slides along $g$ = 1 into the centre.

steps.prompt: To match {{RL|Ω}} to 50 Ω with $|\Gamma|$ ≤ {{Gm}}, you compare a single λ/4 transformer (exact bandwidth formula) with a two-section binomial transformer (small-reflection estimate). By how many percentage points does the binomial design widen the bandwidth?
steps.explanation: Single section (exact): $\Delta f/f_0$ = {{b1}} %. Binomial, N = 2 (small-reflection estimate): |A| = {{abs(RL-50)/(RL+50)}}/4 = {{A2}}, $\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\Gamma_m/|A|}$ = {{0.5*sqrt(Gm/A2)}}, $\Delta f/f_0$ = 2 − (4/π)·arccos({{0.5*sqrt(Gm/A2)}}) = {{b2}} %. Gain: **{{b2-b1}} percentage points**, for twice the length.

steps.prompt: With a complex enough lossless matching network, a load made of R in parallel with C can be matched perfectly over an arbitrarily wide band.
steps.explanation: False. The Bode–Fano limit bounds $\int_0^\infty \ln(1/|\Gamma(\omega)|)\,d\omega$ ≤ π/(RC) for a parallel RC load. A perfect match (|Γ| = 0) anywhere costs infinite area, and a wider band forces a worse |Γ| in that band. Loads with a large stored energy (high Q) can only be matched over a narrow band.

steps.prompt: Match each added element to how it moves an impedance on the Smith chart.
steps.explanation: Series elements change only $x$, so the point stays on its $r$ circle; more $x$ (an inductor) turns it clockwise. Shunt elements change only $b$, so the point stays on its $g$ circle; more $b$ (a capacitor) also turns it clockwise. Capacitors in series and inductors in shunt go the other way.
